source_text: An forte non punit, quod quidem facit prudenter, sed etiam remuneratur famulos praeceptis suis, licet iniustitiam docentibus, obsecutos? Et quid ei profuit invidere, si et iniustas res faciendo eo pervenerunt mortales, quo etiam iustitiam servando venissent? Cumque illis, quos circumvenit, de felicitate nihil pereat, hic tamen benignitatis ac iustitiae conscientia simul et honore privatur. Quanto erat tolerabilius a religionis professione colla subducere quam per tam praerupta, tam exitialia orbitas ducere?
pass_a_gloss: Or perhaps he does not punish, which indeed he does prudently, but even remunerates servants obedient to his precepts, although teaching injustice? And what did it profit him to envy, if by doing unjust things mortals arrived where they would also have come by keeping justice? And when for those whom he circumvented nothing of happiness perishes, he nevertheless is deprived at once of the consciousness of kindness and justice and of honor. How much more tolerable was it to withdraw the neck from the profession of religion than to lead a course through so steep, so deadly paths?
pass_b_english: Or perhaps he does not punish them—which is certainly prudent—but even rewards servants who obey his commands, although those commands teach injustice? Then what did his envy achieve, if mortals arrived by doing unjust things at the same destination they would have reached by observing justice? Those he deceived lose nothing of their happiness, while he is deprived both of the consciousness of goodness and justice and of the honor belonging to them. How much more tolerable it would have been to throw off the profession of religion than to steer a course along such steep and deadly paths!

choices.why: Julian's forensic virtue that renders to each his own, without fraude or gratia (partiality).
rejected: righteousness (Pauline overlay unless the verse forces it)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
